title: 4 days, 6 billion Claude tokens: directing agents inside the Unreal editor
author: simone199615
selftext:
I've been a technical artist for ten years, and my day job is building interactive experiences in Unreal outside the games industry. Last week I entered the Epic AI MegaJam with two teammates: four days, theme "Director's Cut". The agents did the typing. I did the design, the art direction, the technical calls and the review. We shipped Save Your Darlings, a side-scrolling platformer.

You play Death. She is the ending of a game whose players complained that the hero dies, so the developer shipped a patch to remove her. The patch failed, and now he is doing it by hand. Everything is drawn as folded paper: the original game in colour, his patch in unfinished grey.

On day one we built nothing. I asked Claude for ideas, turned down about thirty of them, most of them film sets and clapperboards, and at one point told it to stop agreeing with me. The idea that stayed came from the three of us, brainstorming that evening. A wall chasing the player is what a film would do with "the cut". A game gets cut by unloading a level. So the developer types `unload(scene_12)` on the piece behind you: it loses its textures at the first character, goes to wireframe halfway through the line and is gone when the line ends. Ahead of you he types lines that change the room, and your scythe turns a line into a comment before it runs.

The project rules came before the first asset. The maps use World Partition with one file per actor, so several sessions can work in the same map without overwriting each other's binary assets. One session writes in the editor at a time and one writes the C++. Every tunable value is exposed in the details panel. A room starts as a design sheet with tables of positions and timings, and a script places the actors from the tables. Review is a game-camera screenshot next to the concept, 614 of them on day three, plus a bot that presses real keys and replays the routes after every change. By the last day one Claude Code session on Fable 5.2 built nothing and briefed nine others by trade (construction, lights, sound, backdrops, C++), with most of the building on Opus 5.5.

Afterwards I counted the tokens from the session logs. On my machine alone, Claude Code went through about 6.3 billion in four days: 5.1 billion on Opus and 1.2 on Fable. Almost 99% of that is cached context being read again on every turn, and the output is about 15 million tokens. Read it as how long those sessions ran with a full context, since it isn't a billing figure. My teammate's Codex logged another 660 million.

On the last evening I took the editor back. I played all five rooms by hand and placed the set dressing myself, 56 pieces under the nave of the first room alone.

Windows build, about ten minutes to finish: [https://thegamer-dude.itch.io/save-your-darlings](https://thegamer-dude.itch.io/save-your-darlings)

Art book, with the props in a 3D viewer, the storyboards and what we cut: [https://save-your-darlings-artbook.pages.dev](https://save-your-darlings-artbook.pages.dev/Logo/brandbook/brandbook)

The itch page also links the day-by-day devlog.
